lesson_title: From 2,6 Percent to the Edge of Power
hook_text: In 1928, fewer than 3 Germans in 100 voted Nazi. Two years later it was 18. What changed?
clip_script: 1928. The Nazi Party is a joke. 2,6 percent of the vote. Twelve seats. Its leader, Adolf Hitler, born in Austria, failed art student, war veteran, had tried to seize power in a Munich beer hall in 1923. Police fired. It collapsed. In prison he wrote Mein Kampf: race hatred, Jews as the enemy, living space in the east, one all-powerful leader. Then he changed plans: win votes first. But Germany was doing fine, so no one listened. Then October 1929. Wall Street crashes in New York. American banks want their money back, and Germany's recovery was built on American loans. Factories close. By 1932, about six million Germans have no job. Soup kitchens. Fear. The middle parties look useless. The Nazis promise work, bread, order, pride, and someone to blame. September 1930: 18,3 percent. Same party. Same hatred. Different times.
visual_style: A bar chart with a tiny 2,6 percent bar; a beer hall scene freezes; a book titled My Struggle; a stock ticker crashes; queues at a soup kitchen; the bar shoots up to 18,3 percent.
pacing: Quick facts on 1928, a sharp turn at the crash, a slow rise to the final number.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson for Nazi ideas, the Beer Hall Putsch and why the Depression hit Germany so hard.
